title: Gatorlyte vs Pedialyte: Which Is Better for Hangovers and Hydration?
excerpt: Gatorlyte vs Pedialyte compared: sodium, potassium, and sugar per serving, which works better for a hangover or stomach bug, drinking Gatorlyte with alcohol, honest pros and cons, and when to see a doctor.
metaDescription: Gatorlyte vs Pedialyte: electrolytes and sugar compared, which is better for a hangover or stomach bug, Gatorlyte with alcohol, and when to see a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** Gatorlyte and Pedialyte are much closer than their marketing suggests. Both are low-sugar, higher-electrolyte rehydration drinks, and both sit well above regular Gatorade for replacing salt and fluid. Ounce for ounce, Pedialyte Classic carries a bit more sodium and potassium, and it has a long medical track record, especially for sick children. Gatorlyte has a bit less sugar per ounce, adds magnesium and calcium, tastes more like a sports drink, and is easier to grab at a gas station. For a hangover, either one will rehydrate you about as well as the other. Pick the one you'll actually finish.

**The quick picks:**

- **For a child with vomiting or diarrhea:** Pedialyte (or a store-brand pediatric oral rehydration solution), used the way the label or your pediatrician directs. Gatorlyte isn't made or labeled for young kids.
- **For an adult with a stomach bug or food poisoning:** either works. Pedialyte is slightly closer to a medical rehydration formula.
- **For a hangover:** either one. If Pedialyte's salty, medicinal taste turns your stomach, Gatorlyte is the easy swap.
- **After a hot day of drinking and sweating:** either one, sipped steadily alongside some salty food.
- **If you had two or three drinks and feel fine:** water and a normal breakfast will usually do the job. You don't need either.

> **When to see a doctor instead of reaching for a drink.** Rehydration drinks are for mild dehydration. **Get medical care if** you can't keep any fluids down for several hours, you haven't urinated in 8 hours or more, you feel dizzy or faint when you stand, you're confused, you're vomiting blood or something that looks like coffee grounds, or you have a high fever with severe diarrhea. **Call 911 right away** if someone who has been drinking can't be woken up, has slow or irregular breathing, has a seizure, or has cold, clammy, pale or bluish skin. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, and no drink fixes that. If you drink heavily most days and get shaking, sweating, a racing heart, or see or hear things that aren't there within a day or two of stopping, that can be alcohol withdrawal, which can be dangerous. Tell a doctor or go to urgent care. Check with your doctor before using electrolyte drinks regularly if you have kidney disease, heart failure, or high blood pressure, or have been told to limit sodium or potassium. For babies and young children who are vomiting or have diarrhea, call your pediatrician.

## What Gatorlyte and Pedialyte Actually Are

Both drinks are built on the same idea, which doctors call **oral rehydration**. In the 1960s and 70s, researchers worked out that the small intestine absorbs sodium and glucose together. When the two arrive in the right balance, water follows them into the body, even in someone who is losing fluid fast from diarrhea. The World Health Organization and UNICEF built a standard oral rehydration solution around this, and it has saved millions of lives.

The key point is that a rehydration drink is **not just salty water and not just sugar water.** It's a ratio. Too much sugar relative to salt and the drink rehydrates no better than water, and a very sweet drink can even pull water into the gut and make diarrhea worse. Too little sodium and you're mostly drinking flavored water. That ratio is what separates Pedialyte and Gatorlyte from a regular sports drink.

### Pedialyte

Pedialyte is made by Abbott, the large US healthcare company. It started as a product for children with vomiting and diarrhea, and pediatricians have recommended it for decades. Abbott has since added a lot of adult-aimed versions: AdvancedCare and AdvancedCare Plus (with more electrolytes), Pedialyte Sport, sugar-free versions, powder sticks, and freezer pops.

The classic ready-to-drink formula is close to what pediatric guidelines call a maintenance rehydration solution. Per liter, Pedialyte Classic has about **45 mEq of sodium** (roughly 1,035 mg), about **20 mEq of potassium** (roughly 780 mg), chloride, and about **25 grams of dextrose**, a form of glucose. In a 12-ounce glass, that works out to roughly 370 mg of sodium, 280 mg of potassium, 9 grams of sugar, and 35 calories.

### Gatorlyte

Gatorlyte is Gatorade's "rapid rehydration" line, from PepsiCo. It arrived in the early 2020s because the classic Gatorade formula is built for athletes who need sugar for fuel, and it's light on electrolytes for anyone who's actually dehydrated. Gatorlyte flips that balance: more salt, much less sugar.

Gatorade describes it as a blend of five electrolytes: **sodium, potassium, chloride, magnesium, and calcium**. A 20-ounce bottle has roughly **490 mg of sodium**, about **350 mg of potassium**, about **12 grams of sugar**, and around 50 calories. It's sold in 20-ounce bottles and as powder sticks, and there is a zero-sugar version in some stores. Recipes and flavors change over time, so read the Nutrition Facts panel on the bottle in your hand rather than trusting any website's numbers, including ours.

## Gatorlyte vs Pedialyte: Side-by-Side

Comparing a 20-ounce bottle with a 1-liter bottle is misleading, so here's both drinks scaled to the same 20-ounce serving. Numbers are approximate and vary by flavor and version.

| Per 20 fl oz (approx.) | Pedialyte Classic | Gatorlyte |
|---|---|---|
| Type of drink | Oral rehydration solution | "Rapid rehydration" electrolyte drink |
| Maker | Abbott | Gatorade (PepsiCo) |
| Sodium | ~610 mg | ~490 mg |
| Potassium | ~460 mg | ~350 mg |
| Other minerals | Chloride, citrate (zinc in some lines) | Chloride, magnesium, calcium |
| Sugar | ~15 g (dextrose) | ~12 g |
| Calories | ~60 | ~50 |
| Sugar-free option | Yes, in some lines | Yes, in some stores |
| Typical formats | 1-liter bottles, powder sticks, freezer pops | 20-oz bottles, powder sticks |
| Taste | Many adults find it salty and medicinal | Tastes more like a sports drink |
| Made for young children | Yes, with label directions | No |
| Where to find it | Pharmacies and grocery stores | Grocery, convenience stores, gas stations |

For context, regular Gatorade Thirst Quencher has roughly 270 mg of sodium, 75 mg of potassium, and about 34 grams of sugar per 20 ounces. Next to that, both of these drinks are in a different category. The gap between Gatorlyte and Pedialyte is small. The gap between either one and regular Gatorade is large.

And for reference, the **WHO's reduced-osmolarity oral rehydration solution**, the medical standard for treating diarrhea, has about 75 mEq of sodium per liter. Both Pedialyte Classic (about 45) and Gatorlyte (roughly 36 when you scale up the 20-ounce label) are gentler than that on salt. That's normal for retail drinks meant for mild dehydration in people who are drinking them by choice rather than because they're seriously ill.

### What the numbers mean in plain words

- **Pedialyte has a little more sodium per ounce, about a quarter more.** Sodium is the electrolyte that matters most for pulling water back in and keeping it there. If you've been throwing up or have diarrhea, that edge is real but modest.
- **Gatorlyte has slightly less sugar per ounce.** Both are low compared with soda or regular Gatorade. The difference won't matter to most people, though it adds up if you drink several bottles.
- **Gatorlyte adds magnesium and calcium.** That sounds like a win, but the amounts are small, and short-term dehydration after drinking is mainly about water and sodium. There is no good evidence that the extra minerals make a hangover better.
- **Pedialyte is formulated as a rehydration solution first.** That's why it's the one pediatricians and urgent care nurses name. Gatorlyte is a sports company's take on the same idea, aimed at adults.

## Which Is Better for a Hangover?

For most hangovers, **it doesn't matter much.** Both drinks rehydrate more efficiently than plain water, and the difference between them is smaller than the difference between either one and a regular sports drink.

Here's the part most marketing skips. Dehydration is only one slice of a hangover, and often not the biggest one. Alcohol makes you urinate more because it suppresses vasopressin (also called antidiuretic hormone), the hormone that tells your kidneys to hold on to water. So you do lose fluid overnight. But researchers who study hangovers have found that dehydration and blood electrolyte levels don't line up well with how bad people feel. The headache, nausea, fatigue, and foggy thinking seem to come more from inflammation, broken sleep, stomach irritation, low blood sugar in some people, and acetaldehyde, the toxic chemical your liver makes while breaking alcohol down.

So there is no good evidence that Gatorlyte, Pedialyte, or any electrolyte drink cures or prevents a hangover. What they can do:

- Replace fluid and salt faster than water when you've vomited or have diarrhea
- Ease thirst, dry mouth, lightheadedness, and the part of the headache that comes from fluid loss
- Go down easier than food when you're queasy, especially cold and in small sips
- Give you a small amount of sugar if you drank on an empty stomach and feel weak and shaky

If you had a few drinks and feel only a little rough, water, a real breakfast, and time will do most of the work. Our guide on [how to rehydrate after drinking](/never-hungover/how-to-rehydrate-after-drinking) covers the practical steps, and our [electrolyte drinks for hangovers comparison](/never-hungover/electrolyte-drinks-for-hangover-compared) lines up the wider field.

### When Pedialyte's small edge matters

- **You were sick in the night.** Vomiting drains fluid and electrolytes fast, and this is what Pedialyte was designed for.
- **You also have diarrhea.** The closer a drink is to a medical rehydration formula, the better it holds up when fluid is leaving fast.
- **You're caring for a child or an older adult.** Pedialyte has labeled directions for children and decades of clinical use. Use it the way the label or a doctor says.

### When Gatorlyte is the better pick

- **You can't stand Pedialyte's taste.** The best rehydration drink is the one you keep sipping. A drink that's technically ideal but makes you gag is worse than a slightly less ideal one you finish.
- **You were drinking in the heat.** A day at a ballgame, a festival, or a pool party means sweat losses on top of alcohol. Gatorlyte was built around sweaty, active adults, and its 20-ounce bottle is easy to carry.
- **It's what the store has.** Gatorlyte is in a lot of gas stations and convenience coolers that don't carry Pedialyte. If the choice is Gatorlyte or regular Gatorade, Gatorlyte is the closer match to a real rehydration drink. Our [Pedialyte vs Gatorade comparison](/never-hungover/pedialyte-vs-gatorade-hangover) explains why regular Gatorade falls short.

## Gatorlyte and Alcohol: Before, During, and After Drinking

A lot of people search "Gatorlyte alcohol" wanting to know if they can drink it on a night out or use it as a mixer. Here's the plain version.

**There's no harmful interaction.** Gatorlyte is water, salt, a few other minerals, a little sugar, and flavoring. It doesn't change how your liver processes alcohol, it doesn't speed up how fast alcohol leaves your body, and it won't lower your blood alcohol level. You'll be exactly as impaired as the alcohol makes you.

**Drinking it between alcoholic drinks is fine and can help.** Alternating each drink with a glass of something non-alcoholic slows your pace, and slowing your pace is one of the few things that reliably makes the next morning better. A low-sugar electrolyte drink works for that, but so does water. If you want the details on timing, see our guide on [electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking).

**Before bed and the next morning is where it's most useful.** A bottle before bed starts replacing what you've lost, and another in the morning handles the rest. Sip it rather than chugging, especially if your stomach is unsettled.

**Using it as a mixer is a mixed bag.** There's nothing dangerous about it, and some people like it in place of a sugary mixer. Two cautions, though. A drink that tastes like a sports drink can hide the taste of alcohol, which makes it easy to drink faster than you mean to. And you won't get a rehydration benefit from the mixer, because the alcohol in the same glass is still making you lose fluid. If hydration is the point, drink it alongside your alcohol, not in it.

**Don't treat it as a license to drink more.** No electrolyte drink makes heavy drinking safe or protects your liver. If someone at the party is vomiting, confused, or hard to wake, a bottle of Gatorlyte is not the answer. Call 911.

## Gatorlyte vs Pedialyte for a Stomach Bug or Food Poisoning

Outside of hangovers, the most common reason people compare these two is a stomach bug. The general rules:

- **For adults with mild to moderate vomiting or diarrhea:** either is reasonable. Start with small, frequent sips (a few tablespoons every few minutes) rather than big gulps, and build up as your stomach allows.
- **For children:** stick with a pediatric rehydration solution like Pedialyte, and call your pediatrician for advice on how much to give. Sports drinks, even improved ones, aren't the standard recommendation for kids.
- **For anyone who can't keep fluids down, is very drowsy, or is passing very little urine:** get medical care. Some people need IV fluids, and waiting can make things worse.

## Pros and Cons

### Pedialyte pros and cons

**Pros**

- Formulated as an oral rehydration solution, with decades of pediatric use
- Slightly more sodium and potassium per ounce than Gatorlyte
- Labeled directions for children
- Many formats, including freezer pops that are easier to keep down when nauseated, and sugar-free versions
- Powder sticks bring the cost per serving down

**Cons**

- Many adults find the taste salty and medicinal
- Usually found in the pharmacy aisle, not the convenience cooler
- Bottles can cost more per serving than sports drinks
- The many product lines (Classic, AdvancedCare, Sport, and so on) can be confusing

### Gatorlyte pros and cons

**Pros**

- Much more salt and much less sugar than regular Gatorade
- Tastes more like a familiar sports drink, which many people find easier to finish
- Easy to find in grocery and convenience stores
- 20-ounce bottle is a convenient single serving
- Adds magnesium and calcium, though in small amounts

**Cons**

- A little less sodium and potassium per ounce than Pedialyte Classic
- Not made or labeled for young children
- Usually costs more than regular Gatorade
- The "rapid rehydration" label is marketing. It won't fix the parts of a hangover that aren't about fluid

We don't sell or link to either brand. Both are widely available, and you can compare prices at your local store.

## What About Making Your Own?

If you want a rehydration drink without buying either brand, you can make a simple one at home with water, a pinch of salt, and a small amount of sugar or juice. The key is getting the ratio close and not overdoing the salt. Our [homemade electrolyte drink guide](/never-hungover/homemade-electrolyte-drink) walks through recipes and the mistakes to avoid. For a mild hangover, plain water plus salty food such as soup, eggs, or toast with something salty on it also replaces sodium perfectly well.

## How Much to Drink

There's no one right amount, but a few sensible rules apply to both drinks:

- **One bottle is a good start.** A 20-ounce Gatorlyte or a glass or two of Pedialyte is a reasonable first step the morning after. Add water from there.
- **Sip over 30 to 60 minutes.** Drinking fast on a queasy stomach can bring it straight back up.
- **Watch your urine.** Pale yellow means you're doing fine. Dark yellow means keep going.
- **Don't drink several bottles "to be safe."** More electrolytes than you need isn't helpful, and people with kidney, heart, or blood pressure problems should be especially careful with large amounts of sodium and potassium.

## Going After More Than Dehydration

Because dehydration is only part of a hangover, the bigger wins come from the night itself: eating before you drink, pacing yourself, alternating with water, and stopping earlier. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.

Some people also try supplements aimed at how the body handles alcohol. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research is in animals and lab studies, with only limited human data, so it's promising rather than proven, and there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers on its own. If you want to try it, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much people typically take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. It isn't a replacement for rehydrating, and it doesn't make heavy drinking safe.

## The Bottom Line

- Gatorlyte and Pedialyte are both real rehydration drinks, and both are far better than regular Gatorade for replacing salt and fluid.
- Pedialyte has a little more sodium and potassium per ounce and the stronger medical track record, especially for children.
- Gatorlyte has slightly less sugar, a more familiar taste, and is easier to find.
- For a hangover, pick the one you'll actually drink. Neither fixes nausea, fatigue, or brain fog, because those come mainly from alcohol itself and poor sleep.
- Gatorlyte has no harmful interaction with alcohol, but it doesn't lower your blood alcohol or make heavy drinking safer.
- If you can't keep fluids down, stop urinating, or feel confused or faint, skip the store and get medical care.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is Gatorlyte or Pedialyte better for dehydration?**

They're close. Ounce for ounce, Pedialyte Classic has a little more sodium and potassium and is formulated as an oral rehydration solution, so it has a slight edge when you're losing fluid fast from vomiting or diarrhea. Gatorlyte has a bit less sugar and adds magnesium and calcium. For mild dehydration in an adult, including a hangover, either one works. Pick the one you'll keep drinking.

**Is Gatorlyte good for a hangover?**

It can help with the dehydration part of a hangover: thirst, dry mouth, lightheadedness, and some of the headache. It has much more salt and much less sugar than regular Gatorade, so it rehydrates more efficiently. It won't fix nausea, fatigue, or brain fog, which come mostly from how your body processes alcohol and from poor sleep. There is no good evidence that any electrolyte drink cures a hangover.

**Can you drink Gatorlyte with alcohol?**

Yes. There's no harmful interaction. Gatorlyte doesn't change how your body processes alcohol or lower your blood alcohol level. Drinking it between alcoholic drinks can slow your pace and replace some fluid. Using it as a mixer gives no real hydration benefit, because the alcohol in the same glass still makes you lose fluid, and its sports-drink taste can make it easy to drink faster than you mean to.

**Can kids drink Gatorlyte instead of Pedialyte?**

Gatorlyte isn't made or labeled for young children. For a child with vomiting or diarrhea, the standard choice is a pediatric oral rehydration solution like Pedialyte or a store brand, used as the label or your pediatrician directs. Call your pediatrician for advice on how much to give, and get care quickly for babies or for any child who is very sleepy, not urinating, or can't keep fluids down.

**Does Gatorlyte have more electrolytes than Pedialyte?**

Not per ounce. Gatorlyte lists five electrolytes (sodium, potassium, chloride, magnesium, and calcium), which sounds like more, but Pedialyte Classic has a little more sodium and potassium per ounce, and those are the ones that matter most for rehydration. Labels vary by flavor and version, so compare the Nutrition Facts on the bottles you're choosing between.

**Which has less sugar, Gatorlyte or Pedialyte?**

Gatorlyte has slightly less sugar per ounce: about 12 grams per 20-ounce bottle, compared with roughly 15 grams in the same amount of Pedialyte Classic. Both are far lower than regular Gatorade, which has about 34 grams per 20 ounces. Both brands also sell zero-sugar versions in some stores.

**Is it okay to drink Gatorlyte or Pedialyte every day?**

For most healthy adults, an occasional bottle is fine, but they're designed for times when you've lost fluid, not as an everyday drink. If you're not sweating heavily or sick, water is usually enough. People with kidney disease, heart failure, or high blood pressure, or anyone told to limit sodium or potassium, should check with a doctor before drinking them regularly.
